---
title: Pixi
---

[Pixi](https://pixi.sh) is a package manager that installs the software a
project needs into an environment that belongs to that project. It is
comparable to Conda, but faster, and it records the exact versions that were
installed, such that a collaborator, a cluster or a CI run gets the same
environment as we have locally.

Pixi is not limited to Python packages. It installs from
[conda-forge](https://conda-forge.org), which also provides compilers, command
line tools, LaTeX and Quarto, and it does so without administrator rights. For
this reason the group templates and this handbook use Pixi, and the only
prerequisite for working with any of them is that Pixi itself is installed.

## Installation

On macOS and Linux, run the following in a terminal:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://pixi.sh/install.sh | sh
```

On Windows, run the following in PowerShell:

```powershell
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -c "irm -useb https://pixi.sh/install.ps1 | iex"
```

Restart the terminal afterwards and check that the installation worked with

```bash
pixi --version
```

Other ways of installing, e.g. with Homebrew, are described in the
[official installation guide](https://pixi.prefix.dev/latest/installation/).
Pixi updates itself with `pixi self-update`.

## Working in a project that uses Pixi

A project that uses Pixi has a `pixi.toml` file in its root directory. This is
the case for the group templates, where nothing needs to be set up beyond
cloning the repository.

### Running tasks

A project typically defines *tasks*, which are short names for the commands
that are used often. They are run with `pixi run`, e.g.

```bash
pixi run build
```

The first time a task is run, Pixi installs the environment, which may take a
minute; afterwards it starts immediately. The tasks that a project defines are
listed with

```bash
pixi task list
```

Any other command can be run in the environment in the same way, e.g.
`pixi run python script.py`. Alternatively, `pixi shell` starts a shell where
the environment is active, comparable to `conda activate`, and `exit` leaves it
again.

### Environments

A project can have more than one environment, e.g. one with Python for
producing figures and one with LaTeX for compiling a document. The environment
is selected with `-e`:

```bash
pixi run -e latex build
```

Without `-e` the environment named `default` is used.

### The files Pixi uses

`pixi.toml`
:   The manifest. It lists the packages the project needs, the tasks and the
    environments, and it is the file that we edit, either by hand or with the
    commands below.

`pixi.lock`
:   The lock file. Pixi writes it and it records the exact version of every
    installed package. It should not be edited by hand.

`.pixi/`
:   The directory where the environments are installed. It can be deleted at
    any time and is recreated from the two files above.

Both `pixi.toml` and `pixi.lock` should be committed to git, as it is the lock
file that ensures that everyone gets the same environment. The `.pixi/`
directory should not be committed; the group templates already list it in
`.gitignore`.

## Adding packages

A package is added to the project with

```bash
pixi add numpy
```

which installs it and updates `pixi.toml` and `pixi.lock`. Packages are taken
from conda-forge by default. A Python package that is only available on
[PyPI](https://pypi.org) is added with

```bash
pixi add --pypi <package>
```

In general we prefer the conda-forge version when both exist, in particular for
packages that depend on compiled libraries. A package is removed again with
`pixi remove`, and `pixi search <package>` shows whether a package is available
on conda-forge.

## Starting a new project

When a project does not start from one of the group templates, Pixi is set up
in an existing directory with

```bash
pixi init
pixi add python numpy
```

A task is then added either by editing `pixi.toml` or with

```bash
pixi task add fit "python fit.py"
```

## Tools that are not tied to a project

Command line tools that we want available everywhere, rather than in a single
project, are installed with `pixi global`:

```bash
pixi global install ripgrep
```

Each tool is installed into its own environment, such that they do not
interfere with each other or with any project.

## Further reading

The [Pixi documentation](https://pixi.prefix.dev/latest/) covers all of the
above in more detail, and `pixi --help` lists the available commands.
